## A cheaper masked match: a re-find's dot products by transform (2026-10-26)

The user, 2026-10-26 evening, of perception at its 30 frames a second: it "still doesn't have much good headroom". Three branches, to be tested live that night: fewer re-find matches, a cheaper matching kernel, one C call for a frame's re-finds. This is the kernel's (work/pfast-kernel): the same answers, exactly, for less CPU. The re-finds' masked matches were 17.3-17.6 ms of a crowd frame's work on one thread (below), most of the step. Their dot products, place by place, were already AVX2's integer madd, and at the madd's own pace: 0.42 ns a madd in registers on this Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3: AVX2, no AVX-512, no VNNI), 0.49-0.56 with the loads (D:/MapleHelper-scratch/pfast/kernel/peak.c), so the kernel could only get cheaper by doing fewer products.

**What changed** (`gamelab/native.c`; `mm_best`'s and `mm_match`'s answers the same to the bit, their calls as before):
- *A window's dot products, every place at once, by number-theoretic transform* (`ntt_*`): the correlation of the window's channels with the template's, as the products of their transforms modulo the prime 998,244,353 on 128 x 128 planes. Integers throughout, so the sums are exact (a dot product is at most 255 x the template's sum, which `mm_prepare` checks is under the prime; else that template stays place by place). The window's transform is made once a call for all its templates; a template's transform is made with it (`mm_prepare`: three transforms of a plane, about 0.1 ms), and each template then takes its products and one inverse transform, for its places' columns only. A template goes by transform where its places x its 16-wide chunks (the madds' work place by place) come to 300,000 (`NTT_LEAST`): a re-find's window as it is (98 x 102 around a 52 x 56 picture: 2,209 places, 413 chunks, 912,000), not a step-2 check's (81 places), nor a window past a plane (128 px) either way. On the crowd's re-find windows as recorded and cropped by 8, 16 and 20 px a side (42,530 calls, both ways on each: `pfast/kernel/bench2.c`) the transform was faster in 24% of the calls at a work of 200,000-300,000, in 97% at 300,000-400,000, in all past 600,000.
- *The mask's sums 24 places at a time* in AVX2's registers over all of a row's runs (each channel's prefix sums apart, so a place's sums lie side by side), and *the scores of a transform's places 4 at a time in double*: the same arithmetic to the bit, as N, B and A are integers under 2^53 there and each rounding (A B, the root, the quotient, the float) is IEEE's one rounding, as in the place-by-place code.
- A template made ready carries its transform: 192 KB more a colour template, 64 KB a brightness one. In a run of the step over 01:01's 3,048 frames 122 were made ready, 24.3 MB of them against master's 3.2 (`pfast/kernel/mem_count.py`).
- `mm_ntt(least)` sets the threshold (the tests force either way: 0, or a huge number) and `mm_transformed(template)` says whether one has its transform.

**The answers** (D:/MapleHelper-scratch/pfast/kernel; offline: no game, no keys, no capture, nothing attached to the live services; every job at Idle priority on CPUs 12-23 through `bg_quiet.cmd`):
- *Every call as master's:* the 20,955 masked matches (`mm_best`'s calls: 10,698 re-finds, 10,257 step-2 checks, gates and twins' checks) of the crowd's 600 frames (01:01 [700:1300]), recorded one frame at a time from master's step (`record_calls.py`: its eyes and senses as `feed.saved_world` makes them, `service.SCHEDULE`, the searches inline, the re-finds on one thread, the frames 1/30 s apart, unheld, after 30 frames' warm-up), each call's window, templates, stop and master's answers: the same scores to the float's bit and the same places on every call, through `native.best_matches` (`time_py.py`, 4 runs) and in C alone (`bench.c`), on AVX2 and in plain C (the first 2,000; `mm_simd(0)`); and the transform's against place by place on the windows cropped by 8, 16 and 20 px a side (`bench2.c`: 31,832 calls more, none different).
- *The states as master's:* the step (`ident.py`: as `record_calls.py`, but the re-finds on the 4 threads of the service) with master's DLL and the branch's, a digest of each frame's state (its tracks, monsters, events, the step's counts, her place and tag, and the late states of its searches) on every frame of both Lie Detectors' `before/` (2026-10-26 00:25 and 01:01): 0 of 3,048 frames different in each (01:01: 21,140 re-finds, 4,377 fallbacks on both; 00:25: 26,851 and 5,474).
- *The tests* (`tests/test_native_match.py`): by transform, place by place and in plain C, the scores to the bit and OpenCV's within 3e-5 with its best place, on a re-find's window and picture (colour and brightness), a window the template's size, a picture as wide as a plane with empty mask rows, a whole plane with seven empty rows, one pixel (flat: -1), a picture as tall as its window; a dark 110 x 110 template whose sums of squares need int64 (`wide`), by transform; a template whose dot products could reach the prime, and a window past a plane, place by place; a call stopping at its first picture to reach `stop`, and ties going to the first row by row, all three ways; and the first map's re-finds drawn as the game draws them (`pasted.refinds`), every call by transform against place by place and plain C.

**Measured** (one thread; the re-finds' calls recorded above, each through `native.best_matches`, ctypes and all, the best of 3; master's DLL and the branch's alternated, 2 rounds, CPUs 12-23 57-67% busy with other agents' work; a frame's: the sum of its calls):

| | a re-find call, ms: median / p90 / p99 | a frame's re-finds, ms: median / p90 / p99 / mean | a frame's 35 masked matches (step-2 checks too), mean ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| master | 0.61-0.62 / 1.89-1.94 / 2.45-2.47 | 18.8-19.0 / 25.1-25.9 / 31.0-31.5 / 17.3-17.6 | 18.2-18.5 |
| the branch | 0.31-0.32 / 0.60-0.66 / 0.76-0.83 | 6.5-6.7 / 9.1-9.8 / 10.9-12.0 / 6.2-6.5 | 7.0-7.3 |

  So a crowd frame's masked matches take about 11 ms less of CPU (0.33 cores at 30 frames a second); a re-find call with four pictures (its animation's next frames) costs about what one with one did, as the window's transform is shared (p90 0.60-0.66 ms against 1.89-1.94). In C alone (`bench.c`, each call the best of 3, alternated with master's, CPUs 12-23 62% busy): the 20,955 calls 4.1 s against 10.6, a re-find call 0.28 ms against 0.59 (median), a frame's re-finds 6.2 ms against 17.0 (mean). Of a template's matching by transform (`bench.c` with PROF, before the scores went 4 at a time): the window's transform 0.39 M cycles a call, a template's products and inverse 0.13 M, its sums and scores 0.24 M.

**Left out** (measured): two result rows sharing each image load in the place-by-place madds, 7% faster (10.2 s against 10.9; 11.1 against 12.1); a Cauchy-Schwarz bound on a place's score from the rows not yet summed, to skip places that can't beat the best so far (on 150 of the crowd's re-find matches, numpy, `prune_sim.py`: 68% of the products left even with the best known in advance, 52% with a floor at `THRESHOLD`, which wouldn't be exact as `mm_best` stands).

**For the other branches:** with smaller re-find windows the transform gains less, and the threshold picks place by place by itself where that's cheaper: on the windows cropped by 8 px a side (pad 8) 2.8 s by transform against 4.3 place by place, by 16 (the box itself) 2.0 against 1.2, by 20 1.7 against 0.4 (`bench2.c`, the 10,500-10,700 calls of each). A window of 64 px or less each way could take planes of 64 (a quarter of the work); not built.

## Fewer re-find matches: near first, and a window's last answer (2026-10-26)

The user, 2026-10-26 21:00, on perception at 30 frames a second, which "still doesn't have much good headroom": "Fewer re-find matches" (beside a cheaper matching kernel and one C call for a frame's re-finds: the sections before and after this one). The frame rate stays 30; each frame matches less, for the same answers.

**Where the re-finds' time went** (master bf0a1ba, offline: D:/MapleHelper-scratch/pfast/pfr's `ident.py --stats`, the feed's step on the saved frames one at a time, its searches inline, everything on one thread, every re-find timed and its masked matches counted; `ana.py`). On 01:01's `before/` (3,048 frames, 10 a second as saved) 5.2 re-finds a frame, 14.7 ms a frame on one thread, 21 pictures matched over 36,000 places; on its crowd's [700:1300] 8.5 re-finds, 24.9 ms. Of that time (the crowd's frames each held 3 times, closer to live motion, in brackets): a monster found with its last picture 10% (20%), with its next frames 28% (22%), the kind's whole set (the fallback) finding it 10% (6%) and not 25% (22%), a hidden track's re-find 27% (30%). A re-find's window is its picture's box and REFIND_PAD around (23 px at 1366x768: 2,209 places for a mushroom's 56x51), and where the re-finds found them, a monster's feet were 3-4 px from where they should be (median), 14-17 at 90% and 22 at 99%, frames 0.1 s apart or held (the tracker walks it on as it was; these mushrooms hop and turn; her minimap dot's steps move them all on screen: taken out frame by frame, 14-15 px at 90% stay, `resid.py`).

**What changed:**
- *Near first* (`mobs.near_pad`, `MobDetector.refind`'s `near`, `worldstate.NEAR_FIRST`): each track is looked for first only as far around its box as it can have got since it was last seen: turned at once at its kind's fastest walk (the tracker's SPEED_CLAMP x its speed), twice that walk over the time, and NEAR_MARGIN (4) px more: at 30 frames a second 12 px for a mushroom (625 places against 2,209), at 10 a second 28, no smaller than REFIND_PAD's window, which is then all it looks at, as before. Its last picture and its next frames are matched there as in the whole window; only where none scores over REFIND_GOOD (as rounded: a 0.900 may be under it), or it's another kind's monster, does it go on to the REFIND_PAD window as before (THRESHOLD wouldn't do: a picture cut by the near window's edge can score 0.6-0.9). So the answer can differ from master's only where a place outside the near window scores higher than the one over REFIND_GOOD inside it: on these frames, nowhere. (Since the review, a near answer is taken only at NEAR_GOOD, 0.95, or more: Perception, faster re-finds, After the reviews.) The margin: of 0-10 px tried on the held frames' re-finds as master made them, 4 found 65% of the live re-finds there (57-78%) for 0.66 of the places (0.59-0.84).
- *A window's last answer* (`memo`, exact): each track keeps, from one re-find to the next, its windows (near, whole, the kind's whole set's), what each gave and its pixels; a window at the same place, looked at with the same pictures, whose pixels are the very same, gives that again without a match (the twins' check, `_its_kind`, is made again: it looks past the window). Its cost where it misses: a copy and a compare of the window (about 30 KB).
- *Back to the whole window* (`_far`): where a track's last re-find found it only outside its near window, or not at all, the next goes to the whole window at once (and near again once the whole window finds it inside the near one). Without it, where the motion a frame outran the near window frame after frame (the saved frames stamped 1/30 s apart, their motion 0.1 s's: 3 times live's), near first cost more than it saved (below).
- In plain small functions (`_window`, `_recall`, `_keep`, `_far`, `_inside`, `near_pad`, `_matched`), for the step that puts a frame's re-finds in one C call. The simulator's fakes get neither (`Eyes.refind` hands `near` and `memo` only to a detector that takes them), so its tables are as they were.

**Measured** (the same scripts; master's copy read only, `D:/MapleHelper-scratch/pfast/pfr/ref`; every job at Idle priority on CPUs 12-23, at most two at once, the game up):
- *The states:* every state master's on both Lie Detectors' `before/` (00:25 and 01:01), unheld and each frame held 3 times (1/30 s apart): 0 of 30,013 states differ (4,346, 10,645, 4,399 and 10,623, the late ones included), every one of 138,856 re-finds' answers the same (`cmp.py`, `diffref.py`), the same tracks (134, 124, 157, 155), deaths and whose (37 hers and 10 others' at 01:01, 54 and 28 at 00:25), events, fallbacks and searches; the same without the back-off. (Before the rounding above was set right, 2 held frames of 01:01 differed: a re-find kept a 0.900 at the near window's edge where master's went on to the next frame at 0.99, a px taller.)
- *The matches* (places x the picture's px, the kernel's work, counted exactly): held 3 times, 98.5 -> 55.9 M a frame at 01:01 and 106.1 -> 60.2 at 00:25 (-43%; the crowd's 170 -> 101, -41%; without the back-off 60.5 and 63.7), the places 33,700 -> 19,100 and 36,300 -> 20,600, the pictures matched 18.4 -> 14.0 and 19.1 -> 15.0; of the re-finds, 35% answered in the near window, 26-30% from the memo alone, 8% in the near window and then the whole one, 28-32% in the whole one alone (hidden tracks, the back-off). ## One call for the re-finds: a frame's matches in C, its Python as each comes back (2026-10-26)

The user, 2026-10-26 21:00, beside fewer re-find matches and a cheaper kernel (the two sections above): "One C call for the whole re-find step", the matching moving later to a Direct3D 11 shader (being built apart, behind the same call). The frame rate stays 30; each frame's re-finds take less, for the same answers.

**What changed:**
- *The matches in one call* (`MobDetector.refind_all`, `Eyes.refind_all`, `worldstate.ONE_CALL`; `native.Refinds`, native.c's `rf_*`): each frame the step hands every track's windows (its near one and its REFIND_PAD one: Fewer re-find matches) and pictures (its last, both ways for a cut-out; its next frames, `_next_frames`, as indices into the detector's pictures, made ready once and made a list once for each kind, picture and facing: `_lists_of`) to the C at once, Python's lock let go: there each job is matched on one of REFIND_THREADS threads of the C's own (a pool made once with the detector's context), each window loaded once, its stages as `_matched` takes them (the first pictures, then the next ones till one scores REFIND_GOOD; THRESHOLD and the best so far as rounded: R(s), Python's round(s, 3) worked out in C, `rf_rounded`, every float32 tried the same), the near window first, the whole one where its best doesn't pass REFIND_GOOD (and since the review NEAR_GOOD, `ngood`: Perception, faster re-finds). A window's last answer (the memo) is the C's now, per track and window, kept the same way (its place, its pictures, its pixels byte for byte). Before, each re-find was a task of the step's pool, its Python (windows, slices, list building, `_next_frames` every time, the memo's copies) taking turns at Python's lock with the others', a C call a picture list.
- *Its Python as each comes back* (rf_start, rf_next, rf_end): the C hands the jobs over as they're done, and the step's thread does each one's own part meanwhile, while the others are matched: whether the picture found is its kind (`_its_kind`), the back-off's note (`_note_far`), and where nothing scores, the kind's whole set (the fallback) handed to the step's pool at once. A job not done yet and none to hand over: the step's thread matches one itself. The near window's answer passing REFIND_GOOD but not its kind goes to its whole window in a second call (on the crowd's frames, never), a job the C couldn't do to the Python as before (never).
- *The twins' check, its pictures' side kept* (`_pick_here`, exact): `_its_kind` (every twin kind's re-find: Horny and Green Mushrooms here, 5.6-5.9 a crowd's frame) worked out each time what depends on the pictures alone: which pictures go beside the monster's, each one's mask, its colours there less their mean and their sum of squares, and for the pictures found at their places relative to each other, each one's own parts (a dilation and a stamp each). They're kept now (`_picking`, a dict with the detector), the frame's side of each score worked out as before, so every score is the same to the bit: 2.3 ms a crowd's frame on one thread -> 1.0.
- What stays Python's: the fallback (rare: 1.1-1.5 a crowd's frame), `_its_kind` (in C it would be numpy's float64 sums to the bit), the HP bars, the tracks. Without the DLL, or a frame the C doesn't read as it is, or a detector without `refind_all` (the simulator's fakes), each re-find goes as before.

**The call's contract** is in native.c (rf_open, rf_run, rf_start / rf_next / rf_end, rf_close), for a backend to give the same answers its own way: the jobs (an id, its pictures' key, two windows, two picture lists), each window's best as `_matched` has it, the near window's REFIND_GOOD (and NEAR_GOOD since the review; each job's id its own in a call), the memo optional, and what a GPU can give to the bit (its integer sums; the scores and the first best on the CPU). The matches go through one function (`rf_best`): the cheaper masked match's (`match_loaded`, A cheaper masked match), by transform where that pays, each window loaded once for both its stages with room for the transform if any of its pictures wants it (`rf_wants_ntt`).

## A cheaper whole screen: the monster search's step 1 in C; the GPU measured (2026-10-27)

The user, 2026-10-27 about 14:20, on learning that the perception service re-finds the monsters it follows every frame but looks for new ones on a timer (her band every 0.2 s, the whole screen every second, the drops when asked) because a whole screen is dear, and that a look's ask only brings a search forward to the next frame: "Can we improve the full screen search latency/efficiency? Will using GPU help?" On the CPU, yes, with master's answers: a crowd's whole screen took 115 ms of CPU on one thread and takes 20 (about 1.8 more since the reviews made it master's by construction, below), and on its thread in the service 55-69 ms (median) and now 14-17, the service taking about 0.4 of a core less in a crowd (33-35% as first built; the fix 0.01-0.03 back); an ask for it is answered in 26-28 ms instead of 61-84. The GPU: not built (below): a GPU step 1 with the same answers was built as a probe and measured head to head with this C on the service's frame loop: at today's one whole screen a second it would save about 0.015 of a core, at 8-19 a second 0.06-0.18, each whole screen coming back 7-14 ms later, at the card's idle clocks (P8), where the frame loop's pace leaves it.

**Where a whole screen went** (D:/MapleHelper-scratch/sfast/profile, `stages.py`: 600 frames of 01:01's crowd, master b41d528, its five bands one after another on one thread, ms of CPU a screen; its instrumented copy of the search gave master's answers on every frame): OpenCV's `matchTemplate` of the 180 silhouettes 81.7 of 116 (the slime's 110 shapes 49.0 of it: no slime was found on any of the 3,300 frames sampled), over 4.07 M windows a screen of which the cover test then kept 148 k (3.6%), the others' scores zeroed before the peaks; the cover test and the peaks in C 14.7; the shrink 4.5; the colour tests, the learned gates and the coarse picture 11.7; the places 2.5; the fine gate's 59 and step 2's 80 masked matches 6.9, a call through Python each. On the pool of 6 the same screen took 149 ms of CPU for 41 of wall, 28% more than on one thread: each band's thread waited 8.6 ms of its 42 for Python's lock, mostly coming back from its 300 short C calls.

**What changed** (work/search-fast; the C off, `mobs.SEARCH_C = False`, not built or no AVX2: all as before):
- *`gamelab/search.c`*, a DLL of its own (`native.search_lib`: built as native.c is, same compiler and flags, named for its source's hash; AVX2's intrinsics, so loaded only where the CPU has it, `sr_ready`; native.c is unchanged). Step 1 of a band in two calls, Python's lock let go for each (`mobs._InC`): `sr_step1` tests every kind's colour 16 pixels at a time (the hand-made tests in int16, the learned gates' table gathered), counts each kind's pixels in every 2x2 cell (I4, 0-4; the coarse picture is I4 / 4 to the bit) with its integral images, scores each shape's silhouette only at the windows the cover test keeps and whose score can reach `SILHOUETTE_THRESHOLD`, and picks the peaks by master's rule (at least the threshold, no less than its 8 neighbours); `sr_places` sorts the spots as Python sorts their tuples and picks the places as `mobs._places` does. A window is left out only where an upper bound of its score plus the bound of OpenCV's noise there falls under the threshold (as built, by more than 1e-6; since the reviews `NOISE_K`'s bound, below): bounded from its colour row by row (each silhouette row's most for that much colour, the shapes of a size side by side in int16 lanes), then column by column, then by its exact products a few rows at a time (`CHECK_ROWS`, the rows of most mass first); such a window is no peak and stops none. Of a crowd's windows 148 k a screen pass the cover test (as master's: the profile's 3.6%), and 10 k of them (7%) are scored to the end, the rest left out by rows (36 k), columns (37 k) or early (65 k) (`probe/scored.py`, 150 of the crowd's frames). `sr_shrink` shrinks the band to step 1's scale: OpenCV 5.0.0's INTER_AREA, its float32 arithmetic in its order, the same bytes as `cv2.resize`, which it leaves the scales it doesn't take (1.75 or more, or none, either way).
- *The scores are the exact ones*: a silhouette's values (float32, each a multiple of 2^-shift) as integers, every sum an integer (`mobs._tables` checks a silhouette's bits: its sums under 2^52), N / sqrt(A B) rounded once to float32 (N = n S_IT - S_I S_T, A = n S_TT - S_T^2, B = n S_II - S_I^2), where OpenCV's go through float32 transforms. A flat window scores 0, as OpenCV's does (its `diff2` test). So, as first built, a peak could come or go where two neighbours' exact scores tie (OpenCV's noise keeps one) or lie within its noise, and two spots of one exact score could come in another order: counted below, and on other maps' detectors it made other answers, so since the reviews the shapes where OpenCV's noise could decide are worked out as master does (After the reviews).
- *The fine gate's and step 2's matches* in a few calls to native.c's re-finds (`rf_run`; `mobs._matches`, `_gated`): each match a job of one picture over its own window, threshold -2 so its best comes back whatever it scores (`mm_best`'s, the same matcher: the first highest score row by row), the window and the place `_match_at`'s to the type; a call for each of the gate's tries (`GATE_TRIES`) and one for the checks, in place of 59 and 80 calls through Python. Each thread keeps its own contexts.
- *A whole screen's bands on 3 threads* (`mobs.SEARCH_THREADS`; since the reviews a pool of their own, `MobDetector._bands`, beside master's 6, each making its threads as its jobs come), her band on the caller's thread: the C's CPU hardly changes with the threads (below), the waits for Python's lock do. A re-find's fallback (its kind's whole set in its window, `MobDetector._fallback`) goes through the same step 1.
- Where it can't, the search is numpy's and OpenCV's as before: a silhouette the C doesn't take (over 64 x 256 cells, sums over 2^52, or about flat, where OpenCV scores every window 1) leaves its detector's searches to them, as does a kind with a hand-made colour test search.c doesn't know (the four of `mobs.PALETTES` it does) or a band whose peaks overflow (`STEP1_PEAKS`; its score planes zeroed again). The service says whether it's in use as each run starts and on its 10 s lines while it isn't (`native.search_state`, in the `session` record's `native` too), as `bench-look` does.
- *`perceive --wide-every S`* (`service.pace`): the whole screen every S s whoever is attached. Not by default: every state changes with the pace, and what a faster one does to the hunt isn't measured (below).

**After the reviews** (2026-10-28; D:/MapleHelper-scratch/sfast/review-exact and review-numbers, the fixes' runs in sfast/finish; offline, every job through `bg_quiet.cmd`, one at a time):
- *Exact by construction, not only on the saved frames.* The exactness review compared the C with master's way on Tree Dungeon's frames shifted, mirrored, cut and with sprites pasted on (0 of 114,160 inputs differed), and with every map's detector here over those frames with its sprites blended in: 5 of 14,952 differed. West Rocky Mountain II's (10004021: stumps, red snails, learned gates that light up much of another map's screen) missed a red snail at 1.0, one at 0.913, one in a re-find's fallback window (the track lost) and, at the 1920x1080 window's half size, a dark stump at 0.625; Tree Dungeon's at half size gave two orange mushrooms of one score (0.906) in the other order (a state another). Each was master's float32 noise against the exact scores: a run of windows whose exact scores tie is a run of peaks by master's rule, where OpenCV's noise breaks it into a few, unevenly spaced (10 of a red snail's 12 places on one such run, 6 px apart, master's 9 leaving its 12th to the snail); and two spots of one exact score go by their place where master's go by its noise. Now `sr_step1` gives each scored window the bound of how far OpenCV's score can be from the exact one, `mobs.NOISE_K` n sqrt(S_II S_TT) / sqrt(A B) + `NOISE_ABS` (the window's colour and the silhouette's energy over the score's normalisation), leaves out only windows whose score's upper bound plus that bound fall under the threshold, and flags a shape where some window's standing by master's peak rule can't be told from the exact scores: one OpenCV's could put at the threshold, with no neighbour surely above it and not surely a peak (a run of tied windows, two neighbours within their bounds, a score within its bound of the threshold; `shape_peaks`, `SR_UNSURE`). `mobs._InC` also looks for any two of a unit's spots, sorted as `_places` sorts them, within their bounds of each other. Those shapes are matched as master matches them (`_InC._master`: `_spots`, OpenCV's matchTemplate on the unit's coarse picture, I4 / 4 from search.c, to the bit cv2.resize's), and again any shape whose spot then lies within its bound of one of theirs, until none: each shape's peaks and every two spots' order are then master's, and the places from them (sr_places for a unit that's sure, `_places` for one that isn't). The bound, measured (`probe/noise2.py`: OpenCV's score and the exact one at every window OpenCV puts at 0.30 or more and its neighbours; 5.40 M windows on 354 saved frames of 01:01's crowd and 00:25's and 23:15's `before/`, 0.56 M on the review's West Rocky Mountain II inputs): |OpenCV - exact| at most 1.10e-6 on the saved frames, 1.05e-5 on those inputs (at windows whose colour varies little, the score's normalisation small); NOISE_ABS (2.5e-7) and 4.0 times 2^-24 of the energy term cover every one of the saved frames', 7.5 times the inputs' (the score's own cross-correlation term n S_IT / sqrt(A B) took 5.2 and 11.4: no one constant), and NOISE_K is 32 x 2^-24, 4x the worst seen; `MobDetector.noise_over` counts any peak of a reworked shape where OpenCV's lay outside it (on the saved frames, 0 of the peaks of 16,552 shapes reworked on 5,119 frames, every 3rd of the five Lie Detectors' `before/`). Whether OpenCV's score at a window is the window's alone: changing pixels 40 cells or more away changed it at the window in 19 of 40 tries (`probe/local.py`: some shapes' correlation goes by blocks of the band), so master's scores are had by matching the whole band, a shape at a time. What it costs (`probe/cost.py`, 200 frames of the crowd, one thread, Idle, arms alternated frame by frame): a whole screen 22.6 -> 24.4 ms of CPU, her band 5.8 -> 6.6, 4.1 shapes a frame worked out as master does (the first try, flagging wherever two neighbours lay within their bounds, took 28.6 and 10.7 shapes); answers the same in every arm on those frames. On the five saved inputs the C now gives master's answers, in master's order, and without `_master` it doesn't (`tests/fixtures/search`, cut from them; `test_where_opencvs_noise_decided_the_answer_is_masters`). Again on the saved frames (`run_verify.sh`, `runs/verify`): the states against master b41d528's dumps (both Lie Detectors' `before/` as saved with the drops and without, held 3x and stamped 30 a second; 23:15 as saved, stamped and held; 10-24 23:51 and 10-25 00:55 as saved), 0 of 64,038 frames differ; every field of the whole screen's and her band's answers with the C and without on the crowd's 600 frames, the three folders every 5th and the ten recent clips every 10th, 0 of 4,481 frames differ (20,302 monsters of the whole screen's, 4,757 of her band's); the review's inputs again, every map's detector with its sprites blended in 0 of 14,952 differ (19,725 monsters), Tree Dungeon's shifted, mirrored, cut and pasted-on 0 of 47,160 (88,887 monsters), its sprites alpha-blended in anywhere 0 of 14,148 (24,478), one sprite a px at a time over a grid on 5 backgrounds, three maps' detectors, 0 of 52,000 (49,144), bars and posts of a mushroom's colour in the crowd 0 of 360 (2,119).

## The re-finds' matches on the GPU: Direct3D 11, the same answers (2026-10-27)

The user, 2026-10-26 about 21:00, after the three re-find items above: "Then move the matching to a Direct3D 11 shader instead of the integer CPU kernel (option 2). Work on this on the side." And: "Don't reduce perception fps please." Direct3D 11 is Windows' own (d3d11, dxgi and d3dcompiler_47 in System32, the SDK's headers to build it): nothing installed. Built behind the one call's contract (native.c's rf_*: One call for the re-finds), its answers the CPU's to the bit, and **off by default** (the file `gamelab/lab/GPU`, or `GAMELAB_GPU=1`, turns it on: `native.GPU`), because on this machine it doesn't pay: the RTX 3080 stays at its idle clocks between the frame loop's calls most of the time (P8: 210 MHz, its memory at 405 MHz), where a crowd's frame of matches takes it 5-5.3 ms (and an empty dispatch about 1 ms to come back) against 2.1-2.2 ms on the C's 4 threads at the same pace. Where it answers it does take CPU off the frame loop (0.1-0.27 cores in a crowd with every call its own), but each answer comes later than the C's: the step and a look's wait longer, the frames a second a little lower, and a game's frames on the same GPU queued behind its matches (After the reviews, below). Clocked up (calls back to back) it takes 0.74 ms, the call 1.0 ms and 0.3 ms of CPU against 1.8-1.9 ms and 5.7-5.8; at 30 frames a second that wasn't seen to pay either (below).

**What it is** (`gamelab/gpumatch.c`, included by native.c after its re-find types, and `gamelab/gpumatch.hlsl`, compiled at run time; native.c's own edits are its hooks: a GPU context opened by rf_open while `gm_on` is on, rf_start sending the call to it, rf_next waiting for it, rf_window's matches answered from it, rf_end and rf_close):
- *What the GPU works out:* each place's integer sums as the contract's GPU paragraph has them (STI, S1_c, S2, uint32 for pictures up to 128 x 128): STI in float32 partial sums of at most 64 pixels of a mask run, every one an exact integer under 2^24 (64 x 3 x 255^2 = 12,484,800), each added into a uint; S1_c and S2 from each window row's prefix sums, a run at a time. Then N and B in 64-bit integers of two uints (exact), and an approximate score s~ = N / sqrt(A B) in float32, -1 where B is 0 as in score_at.
- *The answers the CPU's:* of each window's places only those within 2 GM_EPS (2^-13) of its highest s~ come back, with their sums (at most GM_CAND, 32, a window); the CPU scores them as score_at does (int64 N and B, the double, the float32) and takes the first highest row by row (`gm_answer`). s~ is within GM_EPS (2^-14, 6.1e-5) of the float32 score at every place (N and B exact, then about five float roundings: at most 1.8e-7 at all 42.7 M places of the call set's 36,668 pairs, below), so every place that can be the best is among them, and the answer is rf_best's. A window with more (a flat one: every place -1), a picture past 128 px or flat (A 0), anything the GPU didn't answer: that match the CPU's (rf_best), as before.
- *A frame in one submission:* at rf_start, every job's full window with every picture of its two lists that fits it (both stages at once: which ones the stages look at, and the near window's REFIND_GOOD and NEAR_GOOD, are decided on the CPU after, as rf_window decides them), its near window a sub-rectangle of the full one's places (a place's sums are its pixels', whichever window counts it), a window only with a picture to match there and once a call for two jobs' alike, a window the memo will answer not at all (`rf_recall` asked as rf_window asks it first: a call all memo stays the CPU's); the windows' bytes copied into one upload buffer; three dispatches (prep: each window row's pixels and prefix sums; match: 4 places side by side a thread, 64 threads a group; choose: the candidates), two small copies back, an ID3D11Fence's event. rf_next waits on the event (no spinning) at most GM_WAIT_US (6 ms), then hands the jobs over as rf_window finishes each, on the caller's thread, and on the pool's too where the answers leave pairs to the CPU (`gm_rf_cpu_left`: a picture it doesn't take, a region with more candidates than GM_CAND). A crowd's frame: 10-13 jobs, about 45 (window, picture) pairs, 100,000 window pixels, 95,000 places.
- *Never stalls a frame:* the device is made on a thread of its own (0.7 s to "on", the three shaders compiled; rf_open doesn't wait, the calls the CPU's meanwhile; the pictures packed for it on rf_open's thread, 1.4 ms for Tree Dungeon's 50, so the starter never reads the caller's memory); only a hardware adapter (never WARP, the Basic Render Driver: that's the CPU again); d3d11, dxgi and d3dcompiler_47 loaded at run time, so the DLL's imports are as before and a machine without them has no GPU path (and built without the SDK's Direct3D headers, or with GM_NO_D3D, the backend is only off: the rest of the DLL as before); a call not back within GM_WAIT_US goes to the C's threads at once, and so do the next ones for GM_REST_US (1 s) and until the GPU has caught up (nothing is sent while a late call is still on it); a device removed (a driver reset) turns it off for the context's life; past its limits (GM_MAX_*: 1,024 pairs, 2^19 pixels and places a call) that call. rf_close never waits for it: the last of the context and its starter lets it go, the device released on a thread of its own. Its buffers made once, the pictures uploaded once: about 35 MB of video memory; the process's private bytes 127-156 MB more in the replays (the D3D11 runtime and the driver's). `Refinds.gpu_state()` says what it did (calls answered, late, its own time a pass, windows left to the memo, pools woken); the service's status line says it every 10 s while it's switched on (`native.gpu_line`: "the re-finds' GPU on: 1,234 of 2,300 calls answered, ..."; starting; or off and why), `native.state()` only that it's switched on.
- Found on the way: a window's highest s~ reduced in groupshared before one global atomic a group lost a group's now and then with 4 or 8 places a thread (not with 1; on the call set, with 8, 142 of the 34,601 pairs then had more than 32 candidates; never fewer than the best, so never another answer: the CPU matched those). Each thread's own atomic now: none lost. And a group a 32 x 8 tile of places with its window in groupshared took 0.67 ms clocked up against 0.74 (and by the clocks, as much at P8), with a 64 px limit: left out (`gpu/kern/tiled.hlsl`).

**The probe** (`D:/MapleHelper-scratch/gpu/probe/probe.c`, the game down): adapter 0 the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 (10de:2206, 10,051 MB), 1 the Microsoft Basic Render Driver (software: skipped); a device at feature level 11_1 in 206-348 ms; doubles and extended doubles there (not used), ID3D11Device5's fences there; a cs_5_0 shader compiled at run time in 25 ms. One group's dispatch, a copy to a staging buffer and the CPU reading it: 52-72 us median back to back (Map blocking or an event query polled; 102-137 with a fence's event), but 0.78-1.15 ms median, p99 2.1-3.4, at the frame loop's pace (one every 33 ms), the GPU at P8 between (nvidia-smi). Waiting by Map or a polled query spins the CPU all the while (2.8-4.3 M cycles a round trip at that pace), the fence's event doesn't (1.2-1.6 M, the driver's own).

## The re-finds' GPU, twice as fast: its idle clocks, the game's frames first, a frame's matches sent ahead of its look; the capture's copy on a fence (2026-10-27)

The user, 2026-10-27 about 12:30, told why the GPU path stayed off (at 30 frames a second the RTX 3080 idles at P8, where a crowd's frame of matches took it 5 ms against the C's 2): "For the GPU match, how come it's slower? But anyway 2ms v.s. 5ms doesn't seem to make a big issue, the more important thing is how much CPU core it can save, and whether that benefits a smooth riding of CPU tasks." And on "every call has to send the frame to the card": "This feels wrong, isn't the DX capture happening from the GPU directly? The game uses little GPU so it should mostly be fine. You can test the smoothness question directly offline, I think it will pay off to save some CPU cores."

**Where the frame is.** On the card first, as the user says: desktop duplication hands each frame over as a texture there, which capture.py copies into one of its own (the whole monitor) and then copies the client's box off the card through a staging texture (Capturing the game). Every stage of perception reads that copy in main memory; the re-finds' backend has a device of its own and uploads their windows again, 0.2-0.3 MB a crowd's frame, which costs next to nothing. What it paid was the clocks: at P8 a dispatch's round trip is about 1 ms and its passes about 7 times slower than clocked up, and the step waited for both. Matching on the captured texture itself (zero-copy) would be exact, but is for live only: Not done, below.

**Whether the cores it frees make anything smoother: no** (offline, the game down at every check, D:/MapleHelper-scratch/gsmooth/smooth: the service's real frame loop replayed on the crowd 01:01 [700:1300] as saved, 30 asked, the fake tour attached, normal priority on all 24 CPUs, 60 s after 12; beside it, at normal priority, the game's CPU side (4.0 ms of fixed work every 1/60 s), the hunt's decision (5.0 ms every 1/2.2 s), the key player's wait (player.py's code) and a stand-in game on the GPU really presenting (a flip-model swap chain at the display's 60 Hz, a light draw, frame latency 1); five conditions: quiet, a background job of 2 workers at Idle on CPUs 12-23, 24 spinners below normal, 22 at normal leaving one core free, 24 at normal; three rounds, the arms alternated). With every call the GPU's (as first built) perception took 5-8 ms of CPU a crowd's frame less (about 0.15-0.25 cores at 30 a second), and no probe ran any smoother in any condition: in the quiet ones and under below-normal spinners whatever must keep its pace preempts the rest of the 24 CPUs anyway (the probes as with no perception at all); with one core left free the game's late frames were the same (1,413-1,443 of 3,600 against 1,278-1,570) and the hunt's decision slower; under normal-priority spinners every arm was chaotic (perception 15-30 frames a second from run to run). It cost: the step 7-10 ms longer at the median, a look's wait 5-20 ms longer, 1.2-3 frames a second fewer, and 6-8.5% of the stand-in game's frames done more than 8 ms after their submission. Found there: the live babysitter's idle guard (babysit3.ps1: a python whose command line has `spawn_main(parent_pid` goes to Idle within 5 s) demoted pfast's replay.py child, so replays through it weren't at the live perceive's priority (gsmooth/smooth/tools/smooth_replay.py starts it as a plain child; every measurement here through it).

**What changed** (the same answers to the bit throughout; still off by default):
- *The kernel* (gpumatch.hlsl, gpumatch.c): each window row's pixels and prefix sums laid out in 4 planes, column c at plane c % 4 (a warp's threads' places are 4 apart, so a column's loads lie side by side, in a quarter of the cache lines); match reading them through views of their own (read-only, so cached on the way: they were the UAVs prep wrote); the window's pixels packed 3 bytes in a word, the pictures' too and four of them a load; the slide over four columns a step with no moves; prep reading a window row a word at a time (the rows uploaded word-aligned). The sums are integers either way, so every one is the same.
- *The game's frames first* (GM_PRIORITY): the backend's device at the lowest GPU thread priority (IDXGIDevice::SetGPUThreadPriority -7; `gm_priority` for the benches; rf_gpu's `priority`).
- *A frame's re-finds sent ahead of its look* (the switch's `ahead`: GAMELAB_GPU=ahead, or gamelab/lab/GPU saying `ahead`: native.gpu_mode, AHEAD; worldstate.AHEAD_MORE, WorldStep._send_ahead; MobDetector.refind_ahead, Eyes.refind_ahead; feed.Look, the look with its frame's picture; gpumatch.c's rf_ahead, rf_ahead_use, gm_ahead_take, gm_ahead_best). A frame's re-find windows depend on where its look places her (her name tag, her dot, the ropes: WorldStep._box), so as first built they went to the GPU after the look, 5-7 ms into the step, and the step waited for the round trip and the passes. Now at the frame's start each followed monster's full window where the frame before's camera puts it, 2 px wider each side and 6 taller (the camera moved no more on 83-84% of the jobs of both Lie Detectors' saved frames: gsmooth/hide/cover), goes with every picture of its lists: the windows' bytes copied on the step's thread, the rest of the submission (the tables, prep and match, every place's sums and key copied back, the fence) on a thread-pool callback, so the step goes straight on to its look. Its rf_start never waits for them: the C's threads start on the call at once, and each job's pair whose full window lies inside one sent, with the same pictures, is answered from them once they're in (the first thread to see the fence reached maps them): of the window asked, now known, the places within 2 GM_EPS of its highest s~, scored as score_at, the first highest row by row (more than GM_CAND of them, that pair the CPU's). A frame not sent (the GPU still on the last one) is the CPU's. Only at the game's own size (a look's frame is the capture's picture there); the status line says what it did (native.gpu_line: "... frames' re-finds sent ahead, ... in for their calls, ... windows inside the ones sent").
- *The capture's copy off the card on a fence* (capture.Dxgi._copied, COPY_WAIT_MS; `[capture] fence` in config.toml, false by default): after the box's copy to the staging texture an ID3D11Fence (D3D11.4) is signalled and its event waited on, 100 ms at most, then Map, which so doesn't wait by spinning a driver thread. The CPU path's as much as the GPU's.

Now the thread that wins the mapping asks it (`GetDeviceRemovedReason`, or the fence at UINT64_MAX) and turns the GPU off (why 7, as `gm_wait` does): that call's pairs the CPU's, and every later call's. `rf_gpu_fault`'s 4 acts there too: on the crowd's 599 recorded calls (`finish/tools/fallback2.py`, the review's fallback.py with it) the call it hit took 1.7-2.2 ms against the C's 1.7-2.1 at that point, every field the recorded answers'; tests/test_gpumatch.py's new test (with an error sending, 5, beside it) fails on c897877 (the GPU stays on: the next frame sent again) and passes now.

Now the windows' bytes are laid out on the step's thread in a buffer of the context's own (`host`, as the upload has them) and uploaded on the thread-pool callback (`gm_put`) before the submission: rf_ahead's part 0.12-0.18 ms at the median, 0.34-0.54 at most over five passes (`finish/fb`: three rounds alternated with c897877, the C's threads beside each; 5 ms as the look, 25 ms between calls).

## The whole screen 10 times a second (2026-10-28)

(15 times a second since that evening: The whole screen 15 times a second, below.)

The user, 2026-10-28 about 08:20: "Let's change whole screen search to 10FPS" (and before: cores saved, "Don't reduce perception fps please", perception the same between hunts and during them). The perception service searches the whole screen 10 times a second whoever is attached, where it was once a second with her band 5 times a second besides. With the search's step 1 in C a crowd's whole screen takes 16 ms on its thread (A cheaper whole screen), so it keeps up at 30 frames a second: on the crowd's replays of the service's frame loop, 0.26-0.30 of a core more at live's motion (each frame held 3 times; 0.37-0.43 with the recording's own motion, 0.22 on quiet platforms, 0.22-0.44 between hunts), the frames a second as before, and a monster off her band known to a client a median 0.054 s after it shows (p90 0.088) where it took 0.44 (0.99); in her band 0.054 where 0.11. In the harness, with the feed's costs as measured with the C and only the pace differing (master given the simulator's fixed fake whole screen too, after the review), grinding made 5.8% more EXP a minute (48 seeds paired, se 2.0%, t 2.9), the hunt loop 1.7% (se 2.3%, t 0.8), both together 3.8% (96 pairs, se 1.5%, t 2.5), as many touches that hurt (-0.7%, t -0.3); the hunt loop's trips 3.9% longer (t 1.4), their landings within 105 of a monster walking at her 29% more (t 2.8), something to watch live; no death, fall or stop in any run. Where a whole screen is slow (1920x1080, the simulator's scenarios) her band is searched on its own between them, as before (`BAND_STAND_IN_S`, after the review): there, at the README's `--costs measured`, about 5 whole screens a second with her band's 5, as much EXP as master (+1.9%, t 0.9) and 11% fewer touches that hurt (t -3.2).

**What changed** (work/wide-10):
- *`worldstate.WIDE_EVERY_S` 0.1*, both schedules (the hunt's, HUNTING, and `watch`'s, WATCH: the same whoever is attached); `perceive --wide-every S` still tries another pace. Each is due a period after the one before was due (`WorldStep.wide_due`), on the first frame shown then or later: counted from the last one's frame, at 30 frames a second a fourth frame was waited for each time three came a hair under 0.1 s apart (8.6 a second on sfast's replays at 0.1 s; 9.7-10.0 now, and 30 in 3 s on made-up frames jittered by 1 ms where the old rule made 25).
- *Her band's own search* (`BAND_EVERY_S` 0.2) is counted, as it was, from the last search for monsters, a whole screen's too (the whole screen once a second stood in for every fifth band): so with the whole screen every 0.1 s it isn't searched on its own unless asked or the whole screen falls 0.2 s behind (0-0.05 a second on the replays, 3.9-4.0 before). A whole screen stands in for it only when it came back within 0.05 s of its frame (`BAND_STAND_IN_S`, since the review, below): at 1366x768 a crowd's takes 14-20 ms on its thread, so always; at 1920x1080 and in the simulator (78-100 ms) never, and there her band is searched on its own every 0.2 s between whole screens, as before. It isn't the same search: on 3,637 saved frames of five recordings (`D:/MapleHelper-scratch/wide10/build/tools/bandcmp.py`: each frame placed as the service places it, her band searched and the whole screen, the screen's monsters kept to her band as a look keeps them), of the 4,003 monsters her band's search found the whole screen found 3,756 (94%) at the same spot, 145 at another spot, 15 just past her band's rows and 87 (2.2%, a median score 0.79) not at all, and it found 112 in her band the band's search didn't (2.8%, a median 0.95); 347 of the frames differ. Over time it makes no difference: with her band's own search kept every 0.2 s beside the whole screen (each frame due both searched both ways, the band's monsters that overlap none of the screen's added: `truth.py`'s `b01b`, below), every monster of the truth was first followed as soon, in her band a mean 0.028 s after it showed against 0.029, none never. So it isn't searched beside (it would cost about 0.03-0.04 of a core).
- *The schedule's whole screens take at most half the searches' thread* (`WIDE_SHARE` 0.5): the next waits until the last one's search (with what was searched with it) took at most half the time since its frame. On Tree Dungeon at 1366x768 it binds only after a search of every platform's drops (on the replays 0-4 frames a minute of 2,000 put off hunting, 16-58 between hunts, `watch`'s every 2 s, where the whole screen comes 9.7-9.9 times a second: 'wide put off'); at 1920x1080 on the first map's 17 bench frames a whole screen took 78 ms inline (bench-look, under load) and the simulator's `feed.COSTS` has 100 on the thread: there about 5 a second, the thread half free for what's asked, where 10 would have left it nothing else.
- *Drops asked for go first, alone* (`ASKS_FIRST`): what the schedule has due then (the whole screen, her band) waits for the next frame the searches are free. As first built (the whole screen due with the ask on a third of the frames, and the look waiting for it too) her drops' looks waited a median 29 ms on the crowd's first round against master's 24, those with every platform's drops 118 against 98; with it 23-26 and 98-112. A look asks for her band or the whole screen only when stale (feed.ASK_ONLY_STALE): those go with the drops.
- *The service's 10 s line* says the searches a second since the line before ("searched a second: the whole screen 9.9, her band alone 0.0, the drops 1.2": `Publisher._searches`), its first line the schedule ("the whole screen searched every 0.1 s"), and the session record has it (`schedule`).
- *The simulator*: its feed follows the schedule (Schedule()'s defaults, `SyncFeed`), a search's time in it is its simulated cost (`TimedSearches.take` sets Found.took, for WIDE_SHARE), and its fake whole screen finds every monster wholly inside the rows searched (`FakeDetector.detect_wide`): its bands overlapped by 30 rows, so a monster taller than that across an edge was missed, which her band's own search had covered (fight_step_wall's Orange Mushrooms 60 above her were never found), where the real one's overlap by its tallest picture finds it. `feed.COSTS_1366` (the harness's `--costs measured-1366`) fitted again on these replays with the C (her place 5.0 ms, a re-find 0.27, a fallback 0.6 more, beside 2, her band 7.4, the whole screen 13, a strip of drops 6; until then 70 ms a whole screen, so 10 a second would have taken 70% of the simulated thread where it takes 13% live). `feed.COSTS`, the scenarios' (the first map's 1920x1080 frames), is as it was: there the whole screen comes about 5 times a second.
- Where the docs and comments said "the whole screen every second" for the service (its module, `service.SCHEDULE`, `pace`, `feed.MOBS_FRESH_S`/`WIDE_FRESH_S`, tracking's header, `perceive --wide-every`'s help, The perception service's schedule): now 10 a second. `WIDE_FRESH_S` (0.5) and `MOBS_FRESH_S` (0.3) are as they were: with the whole screen every 0.1 s no look asks for either (the replays' looks asked for no search of their own; master's whole-screen looks asked 7 a minute, waiting 23-28 ms), and they still bound a look's freshness if it falls behind. The drops' schedule is as it was.

The flickers (a whole screen's match seen a frame or two: 40% more in the harness, 2-3 times as many on the replays) and the tracks not seen in their frame are most of the extra re-finds; not publishing a whole screen's lone low-score match until a second sighting confirms it would cut them, a frame later for a real monster scoring low (the user's call: below). Other maps' goldens (the first map's, West Rocky Mountain II's) aren't checked: every scenario's feed searches otherwise now. *Since 2026-10-30 the whole screen is searched in every frame's pass at the service's 15 frames a second, beside her look (Perception at 15 frames a second, one pass a frame): the schedule, her band's own search and `perceive --wide-every` below are gone.*

The user, 2026-10-28, of the 10 a second's numbers: "Yes please add [the whole-screen search's time to perception's 10 s status line], and with this numbers I'm trying to bump the fps to 15 from 10", and, as before, "Don't reduce perception fps please". The perception service searches the whole screen 15 times a second whoever is attached, every other frame at 30 a second, where it was 10 since that morning (The whole screen 10 times a second, above). It keeps up: on the crowd's replays of the service's frame loop the frames a second are as at 10 and as master's (30.0 between hunts, 31-33 hunting with the looks' own frames), 14.3-14.9 whole screens a second hunting of the 15 asked (13.5-14.2 between hunts, `watch`'s drops searched beside), the searches' thread 32-37% busy in a crowd (22-25% on quiet platforms), her band's own search never needed hunting (0-0.3 a second between hunts), for 0.20-0.25 of a core more than at 10 a second at live's motion (each frame held 3 times; the means of 3 rounds, hunting and between hunts; the placebo, the same branch again, -0.01 and +0.07), 0.21 with the recording's own motion, 0.13 on quiet platforms; a look waits 2-3 ms longer for her band (the step about 1 ms longer at the median). **What changed** (work/wide-10-m: work/wide-10's four commits rebased onto master 4558f61, the regular attack's key check, and on them):
- *`worldstate.WIDE_EVERY_S` 1/15*, both schedules (the hunt's, HUNTING, and `watch`'s, WATCH): every other frame at 30 a second, each due a period after the one before was due (`WorldStep.wide_due`, as at 10), so frames stamped a hair early or late still make 15 (44-46 in 3 s of frames jittered by a millisecond). `perceive --wide-every S` still tries another pace; its help and the service's first line say the default ("the whole screen searched every 0.0667 s (15 a second)"). The rest of the schedule is as it was: `WIDE_SHARE` 0.5 (the next whole screen waits until the last one's search took at most half the time since its frame: half of 1/15 s is 33 ms, over a crowd's 16-25 ms at 1366x768, so it binds only after a whole screen searched with every platform's drops; at 1920x1080, 78-100 ms a whole screen, about 5 a second as at 10), `BAND_STAND_IN_S` 0.05 (a whole screen back that soon counts as her band's search: at 1366x768 always), `ASKS_FIRST` (drops asked for go first, alone; the whole screen due then goes on the next free frame, the one after on time, two back to back), feed's `MOBS_FRESH_S` and `WIDE_FRESH_S`.

## Memory and disk

A hunt runs for hours, and perception is to run all the time, so what the stack keeps has to stay bounded.

- **Monster speeds:** `Tracker.speeds` (what `nav` sums up as the speeds seen) keeps the latest 400 of each kind (`SPEED_SAMPLES` in `localization/monsters.py`). Kept all, one a monster a look, a look every frame would add about 110,000 an hour.
- **The drop store** (`behavior/ledger.py`) drops a pile 5 minutes after looks have seen it gone (`GONE_KEEP_S`); kept for ever, every kill added one, and every look went through all of them. The hunt loop's count of the piles she went for that were seen gone (its progress, for the stuck guard) is kept apart (`DropStore.gone_tried`), so it decides exactly as before. In the simulator's hunt loop (preset `game`, seeds 0-2, 20 minutes each) the store ended with 77, 82 and 112 piles instead of 280, 257 and 338 (at most 90-123 at a time), with the same EXP and the same counts after every look. Piles never seen gone, on platforms she didn't look at again, stay: 6-20 at the end of those runs.
- **Telemetry** (`gamelab/telemetry.py`): live hunting wrote 72 KB a minute (4.2 MB an hour; the looks' `scene` records the most of it, 21 KB a minute at 257 bytes each), and a feed of 10 looks a second would write 10-15 MB an hour, in one file per run that was never deleted. A run's file now goes on in a new part past 64 MB (`MAX_BYTES`): a file of its own, named for the time the part starts and always later than the part before, so it sorts after it; its first record is the run's session record with `continues` (the part before's file name) and `part` (2, 3, ...). The part being written is the file written to last, so the mini-map window and the web page (`telemetry.newest`, by last write) go on to it, the rest of the part before read first, without starting over (`ui.sources.LiveSource`: a file whose first record `continues` the one followed isn't a new run). They had started over at each part, as at a new run, and lost what a run sends once: the tour's and the hunt loop's safe platforms and grounds, coloured on the page, with her trail and the log. On NTFS the last write os.scandir reads is the directory's copy, brought up to date only when a file is opened or closed: a part still being written that nothing else opens shows as written when it was made, 0 bytes long. A tour that finished after `watch` began so stayed the newest until `watch`'s part closed, hours later, the page frozen on it. `newest` asks os.stat of the files the directory says were written in the last 7 days (`RECENT_S`; a part is open for 15 hours at most, hunting), and `prune` of every file, which had counted such a part as empty. When a run starts, and again each time a run goes on in a new part, the oldest telemetry files are deleted until the rest take at most 2 GB (`KEEP_BYTES`; `prune`, never the part being written); it says so when it deletes any. None is deleted for its age (`KEEP_DAYS` is None; a number of days would delete files last written longer ago too): live telemetry is evidence that later fits go back to (the terrain and geometry fits of 2026-10-20 were made from the live runs of 2026-10-19 and 20), and small old files cost next to no disk (the first two days of live runs were 38 files and 2.9 MB). The size cap alone bounds the disk. Pruning only at the start had let a run left going for days, such as `watch`, grow the folder without bound. A file another run is still writing can't be deleted on Windows and is left.
- **The Lie Detector's recordings** (`lab/lie_detector`, a folder a cycle: see The Lie Detector's recordings): about 175 MB a cycle answered in 2.5 minutes, at most 700 MB (the 10-minute cap), at 1366×768; half as much again at 1920×1080. When one starts, the oldest go until the rest take 10 GB (`lie_recorder.KEEP_BYTES`; about 58 such cycles), never the one being written: the folder holds 10 GB and the one being written at most. With the rolling recorder's 5 minutes before each (`before/`), about 0.8 GB a cycle answered and 12 of them: the recorder prunes to the 10 GB too, the parts counted, whenever it writes one, as a player older than 2026-10-24 doesn't count them.
- **The rolling recording** (`control/rolling.py`; see The rolling recording): at most 4 GB of frames in memory (`MAX_BYTES`; 2.2 GB for its 5 minutes at 1366×768, kept losslessly since 2026-10-25; 1 GB, 650 MB, a 712 MB process, as JPEG before; in the perception service since 2026-10-26, 15 frames a second each kept as its difference from the one before: on lossless frames 1.1-1.6 GB for 5 minutes of hunting, 0.5 answering a Lie Detector; on the replays' JPEG frames 1.27 GiB after 300 s at 11.6 a second kept in a crowd, about 1.6 at 15, 2.7 on the quiet ones; the floor's own grabs whole, 2 GB for 5 minutes of them; the service's process that much bigger), and a save being written holds the frames it took until they're written. The alarms' clips, PNG, keep 30 GB in `lab/alarm_clips`. On disk, `lab/recent` keeps 5 GB besides the newest save (`RECENT_KEEP_BYTES`), and the part before each Lie Detector counts in the Lie Detector's 10 GB, pruned to by the recorder as it writes one (and by the player as a recording starts, if its code is new enough to count the parts).
- **The player's log** (`lab/player.log`): about 40 bytes a plan, some 150 KB an hour of hunting, never cut. When the player starts, a log past 5 MB is moved to `player.log.1` (the one before goes) and a new one begins (`LOG_MAX_BYTES` in `control/player.py`; the standard library only, so the elevated player loads nothing more).
- **Cancel files** (`lab/inbox/<plan id>.cancel`): a plan cut short as it ended left its cancel file for good (25 had piled up, the player deleting them only when it starts). Now no cancel file is made for a plan that's over (the player renames a plan to `.running` when it takes it and deletes that only once its keys are let go of), and reading a plan's result deletes its cancel file (`control/client.py`).
- **What's there:** `python -m gamelab lab-usage` sizes each kind. On 2026-10-20 the main `gamelab/lab` held 1.5 GB: recordings 1.2 GB (64, made only on request: `--record`, `combo`, `calibrate`), screenshots 277 MB (255), golden traces 2.2 MB, telemetry 2.8 MB (38 files), harness runs 0.5 MB, the rest 0.4 MB. Recordings and screenshots are measurement evidence and are never deleted for you (the Lie Detector's recordings past their 10 GB, when one starts).
- **Soak runs** (`python -m gamelab.sim.soak frames|sim [--minutes 10] [--no-trace]`; minutes long, so not in pytest): the stack kept going offline while Python's allocations (tracemalloc) and the process's private bytes are sampled every 10 s; after a warm-up (the first fifth) it gives the growth an hour on the samples' line and what grew, by line and by part of the code. Telemetry goes to a temp folder in parts of 1 MB, so rotation runs too. Measured on 2026-10-20, other work sharing the CPU:
  - `frames`, 10 minutes: 5,900 real looks at the 17 saved frames (each frame 30 looks in a row; every 5th look with the drops on her platform, every 30th the whole screen; after each the hunter's listeners, the monster tracker, a glance and telemetry). Python's memory was 152.8 MB after the warm-up and 153.0 at the end, +0.4 MB an hour on the line. Of the 198 KB the stack gained, 145 KB was one line of the monster search's spot lists, the same after 1 minute as after 10 (freed tuples Python keeps for reuse), and 14 KB the ledger's 151 kills (about 100 bytes each, kept for the whole hunt). The private bytes moved between 230 and 262 MB as the big looks came and went.
  - `frames --no-trace`, 30 minutes: 29,184 looks (16 a second). Private bytes 197-237 MB, the first third's mean 219.0 and the last's 221.9: +8 MB an hour on the line, inside that swing. A run of hours would tell a slow creep in OpenCV or numpy from noise.
  - `sim`, 10 minutes: 5.6 simulated hours of the hunt loop (seed 0, preset `game`; 1,197 kills of hers). The stack grew 100 KB in the last 4.5 hours, the ledger's kills; the simulator's own lists of every plan and log line grew 8.9 MB, which a real run doesn't keep. At the end the drop store held 112 piles (7 not gone), the landing cache 2,721 entries (2,718 once the planner is built), and telemetry had gone through 30 parts.
- **Still kept for the whole run:** the ledger's kills (about 100 bytes each, 200-400 an hour; `hunt.py` counts them by their index), and piles never seen gone.
- **The continuous feed** (see Continuous perception) holds a fixed amount: 4 frames in shared memory, the last 8 states, at most 10,000 events not drained, only monsters seen in the last 10 s. `soak feed` (the real child on the saved frames, the stack's side asking as a fight does, 15 minutes): the stack's side's Python memory 17.7 MB after the warm-up and 17.9 at the end, its private bytes 66.5 and 67.2; the child's private bytes swung between 156 and 197 MB; 6 minutes more after her band's search went by time, 66.5 and 67.3 MB on the stack's side, and the child's last third's mean 175.3 MB against its first's 181.4 (162-196). The step itself under tracemalloc for 8 minutes in one process: Python's memory 2.0 MB throughout, the private bytes' last third 183.9 MB against the first's 193.1 (161-199 as the big searches came and went). `watch` writes about 16 MB of telemetry an hour (see Continuous perception). With the searches on a thread of the child's own (2026-10-21), 15 minutes of the same with the CPU busy with other work: the stack's side's Python memory 11.8 MB after the warm-up and 12.9 at the end (0.9 MB of it the soak's own record of each state's times, kept for its report), its private bytes 58.4 and 63.4; the child's private bytes 180.5 and 182.0 (165.9-186.3; the first third's mean 179.9, the last's 182.1).

## Limits

- **Recalibrate** after moving the game window, changing maps or changing resolution (each client size keeps its own calibration). Her name-tag template is kept between calibrations; `calibrate --fresh` rebuilds it, and should be run where no rope crosses her name (at 1366x768 on West Rocky Mountain II the name tag finder doesn't find her tag over the clouds: pass `--tag X,Y`; see Screen size).
- **`hunt` needs a 1920×1080 or 1366×768 game window** with a calibration at that size, and the size it had when the command started (see Screen size). The combo analysis on recordings (`track.airborne`'s lift, the claw's swing boxes, `scroll`'s strip and patches, `analyze.UP_PX`) converts its px, measured on the 1920×1080 window's half-size recordings, by the recording's geometry; no recording at 1366×768 has been made to check them on.
- **Each new monster type needs a colour gate** before its game sprites are used: a body-colour test in `PALETTES` in `perception/mobs.py` (the first map's four), or one learned against its map's background colours, which `learn-colours` measures on saved frames of the map (see Perception: learned gates). Its templates come from the game data automatically.
- **Her name tag can be hidden** behind screen widgets at the map's edge, like the party HP box. She's then placed on screen from the minimap dot and the camera, which is only good to about 11 map units.
- **Camera correction for recordings needs ground with a pattern** under her, like a girder or tiles. Plain ground can't be tracked.
- **Swing detection is tuned to the claw's white/lavender swing effect.** Other weapons or skills may need `SWING_MIN_PIXELS` in `analysis/track.py` adjusted.
- **Lucky Seven costs 11 MP a cast at her skill level 10** (the game data; config.toml `[character] lucky_seven`). A 32-shot test uses about 350 MP. Use `--regular-attack` for long runs. Hunting throws Lucky Seven but to finish a monster and while her MP is under a cast (`--attack choice`, the default); `--attack regular` throws the regular attack only.
- **How far above or below a star reaches** beyond 60 units isn't measured. `hunt shots` sums up the shot log.
- **Other players** hunt this map too. Platforms are often empty, and stops then end with no kills. Their minimap dots are seen (Other players), but only inside `MINIMAP_BOX` (300 px wide: this map's minimap; Kerning City's runs past it), and two within 4 game px (46 map units) of each other read as one. Nothing yet knows how much of a ground they take, so the hunt loop doesn't steer clear of them (`hunt.PLAYER_DISCOUNT` off), nor leave the piles by them (`hunt.PLAYER_PILES` off). Their dots are followed from look to look; which marker the game draws over which (hers or theirs) isn't known.
- **EXP from anything else** isn't a kill when no kill of the map's monsters gives that much (Her EXP number), but a share of 2, 4, 6 or 8 is taken for snails, and one that adds up to kills for those kills. Kinds that give the same EXP can't be told apart by it. The EXP table (meowdb.com's) is checked at levels 19 and 20 only. At another EXP rate (an event, a coupon) the sizes go off after 8 kills and each change is one kill, kinds not named, until `gains.EXP_RATE` is set to it. A kill in the very look the cursor comes over the number or leaves it is taken with it (its EXP counts, the kill not).
- **Loot templates cover the drops of the maps `perception/drops.py` knows** (the first map's, Tree Dungeon's and West Rocky Mountain II's: Perception, drops of each map); another map's monsters need their drops added there from their meowdb pages, and the drops' prices to `looting.PRICES` (a test checks them against the game data). Equipment, scrolls, and bills and sacks of mesos aren't looked for; she still picks them up when she walks over them. Nor do they have a price in the hunt loop's table: a kind the detector named that isn't there would count as worth the first map's dearest drop, 50.
- **The full-inventory message** is "You can't get anymore items." It's in the client, not the data files, so `loot.py` matches that and the usual other wordings. Without the OCR packages, only the 3-in-a-row rule tells.
- **The simulator is a model:** its timings and physics are fitted to gamelab's own measurements, its monsters are pushed back by a hit as far as one recording measured and never leave their platform, and its perception is exact unless a scenario adds noise. Use it to check that a change does what was meant, then confirm in game.
